newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mideast violence shakes world, Netanyahu blamed.
newsitem.headline: Mideast violence shakes world, Netanyahu blamed.

text.p: World governments voiced alarm at an explosion of Israeli-Palestinian violence on Thursday and most, well beyond the Arab world, blamed hardline Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu for provoking a second Intifada.
The United States, Russia, France and Britain all appealed for calm and urged Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to return quickly to peace negotiations.
Arab states hailed what they called "the Intifada of the Palestinian people" and said a tunnel Israel had opened in Arab East Jerusalem was part of a plot to destroy a Moslem shrine.
Washington, Israel's closest ally and the dominant power in the Middle East, initially avoided apportioning responsibility for the worst bloodshed since the 1993 Israel-PLO peace accords.
But European and Arab nations pinned the blame squarely on the Jewish state's hawkish 100-day-old government.

By late Thursday, 40 Arabs and 11 Israelis had been killed in two days of widespread violence. Israel declared a state of emergency in the West Bank and Gaza Strip and sent in tanks and helicopters to quell the unrest.

Television images of the bloodshed topped European newscasts and recalled the worst days of the 1987-93 Intifada (uprising), in which Palestinians rose up against Israel's occupation of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The White House said the violence was "cause for great concern" and President Bill Clinton would make a statement on the situation later on Thursday.

The United States mounted a frantic diplomatic effort to defuse the confrontation and urged both sides not to raise new issues that could scuttle fragile peace talks. A further blow-up could also weigh on Clinton's re-election campaign.

Russia, co-sponsor with Washington of the Middle East peace process, said: "The fact that the Israeli authorities, in a unilateral fashion, opened a tunnel next to a Moslem holy site provoked a spontaneous protest by the Palestinian population."
France said Israel's decision to open the disputed archaeological tunnel in the Old City of Jerusalem "led, as was to be expected, to demonstrations which gave rise to violence."

President Jacques Chirac, a day after meeting Netanyahu in Paris and urging him to avoid provocations and return to the land-for-peace negotiations launched by his Labour predecessors, telephoned Arafat to express his "solidarity and support" with the Palestinians and appeal for calm.

The British Foreign Office urged Israeli and Palestinian leaders to show statesmanship and said: "Actions such as the opening of the tunnel along the Western Wall and the recent demolition of a Palestinian community centre in Jerusalem have cause suspicion and disquiet."
The violence wrecked Netanyahu's quest for European support, and forced him to cut short a three-country tour of Britain, France and Germany and rush home to handle the crisis.

Diplomats said there was concern that the explosion of Palestinian anger after months of perceived procrastation and humiliation by Israel could run out of control and trigger wider violence, possibly drawing in Lebanon and Syria.

"Many governments think Netanyahu is getting what he deserves for reducing the peace process to a crawl, going back on the agreement to withdraw from Hebron and resuming Israeli settlement in the West Bank. But the implications are frightening," said one European Middle East-watcher.

Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal, whose country brokered the 1993 Israel-PLO peace accords, told Reuters: "The broad unrest is a signal of the deep frustration among many sectors of the Palestinian community as a result of the lack of progress in the peace process.
"The tunnel and many other items are not large themselves but add together to heighten frustrations and lead to the sort of broad unrest we are seeing now."
